Q9012.L1t: Sociologists and psychologists study how attitudes toward social groups form and shape the way people treat one another.
Q9012.L2t: Welfare recipients are a social category, and generalizations about such groups are a common subject in the study of group attitudes.
Q9012.L3t: The spectator only voices a negative belief about a whole group, and no action toward any member of that group is described.
Q9012.L4t: The spectator's exclamation is a prejudgment, an unfounded negative attitude about a group, so it is prejudice.
Q9012.L2f: Studies of attitudes toward welfare recipients show that most people hold no generalized views about them at all.
Q9012.L3f: The spectator's exclamation counts as an act that treats welfare recipients unfairly, since a spoken statement is a form of unequal treatment.
Q9012.L4f: The spectator's exclamation is discrimination, because it expresses a negative judgment of a group out loud.

Q9013.L1t: Misrepresentation is a tort claim that concerns false statements made by one party to another in dealings such as settlement negotiations.
Q9013.L2t: The adjuster knowingly told the pedestrian something false about the pedestrian's legal rights, and the pedestrian did not accept the offer.
Q9013.L3t: A misrepresentation claim requires that the plaintiff suffered actual damages from relying on the false statement, and the pedestrian rejected the offer, hired a lawyer, and recovered the full jury verdict.
Q9013.L4t: The pedestrian will not prevail, because the false statement caused the pedestrian no monetary loss.
Q9013.L2f: Insurance adjusters are generally forbidden by state law from discussing the merits of a claim with an injured person.
Q9013.L3f: A misrepresentation claim can succeed only if the defendant owed the plaintiff a special duty of trust and loyalty, and an adjuster for the other side owes none.
Q9013.L4f: The pedestrian will not prevail, because the adjuster had no fiduciary relationship obliging him to protect the pedestrian's interests.

Q9014.L1t: Felony murder is a doctrine that makes a death during a dangerous felony murder even without intent to kill.
Q9014.L2t: Courts have taken different approaches to felony murder, and many have narrowed it through limits on causation and on who may be the victim.
Q9014.L3t: Under the prevailing modern approach, the agency theory, felony murder liability attaches only when the killing is done by a felon or someone acting in concert with the felons, and a police officer is neither.
Q9014.L4t: The appellate court will likely reverse, because most jurisdictions do not apply felony murder when a third party kills a co-felon.
Q9014.L2f: Felony murder was abolished in most states after courts found that it conflicted with constitutional due process requirements.
Q9014.L3f: Under the prevailing modern approach, the proximate cause theory is universally adopted, so every death that results from the felony is attributed to the felons regardless of who fires the fatal shot.
Q9014.L4f: The appellate court will likely affirm, because every state holds felony murder applies to any death during the crime no matter who fired the fatal shot.
